entries.3dc9cda3422de8aecf270003f505eb5aff53e2e5: <div sID="gen15057" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="9" osisID="Eccl.9" sID="Eccl.9"/> <div eID="gen15057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15058" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15059" type="x-p"/> Solomon, in this chapter, for a further proof of the vanity of this world, gives us four observations which he had made upon a survey of the state of the children of men in it:—I. He observed that commonly as to outward things, good and bad men fare much alike, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.1-Eccl.9.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. That death puts a final period to all our employments and enjoyments in this world (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.4-Eccl.9.6">ver. 4-6</reference>), whence he infers that it is our wisdom to enjoy the comforts of life and mind the business of life, while it lasts, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.7-Eccl.9.10">ver. 7-10</reference>. III. That God's providence often crosses the fairest and most hopeful probabilities of men's endeavour, and great calamities often surprise men ere they are aware, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.11-Eccl.9.12">ver. 11, 12</reference>. IV. That wisdom often makes men very useful, and yet gains them little respect, for that persons of great merit are slighted, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.13-Eccl.9.18">ver. 13-18</reference>. And what is there then in this world that should make us fond of it?
entries.8074c9e41f416d9474be460f7cd7a7db1fe7c83b: <div eID="gen15059" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15058" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Mysteries in Providence.</title> <div sID="gen15060" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> For all this I considered in my heart even to declare all this, that the righteous, and the wise, and their works, <hi type="italic">are</hi> in the hand of God: no man knoweth either love or hatred <hi type="italic">by</hi> all <hi type="italic">that is</hi> before them. <hi type="super">2</hi> All <hi type="italic">things come</hi> alike to all: <hi type="italic">there is</hi> one event to the righteous, and to the wicked; to the good and to the clean, and to the unclean; to him that sacrificeth, and to him that sacrificeth not: as <hi type="italic">is</hi> the good, so <hi type="italic">is</hi> the sinner; <hi type="italic">and</hi> he that sweareth, as <hi type="italic">he</hi> that feareth an oath. <hi type="super">3</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> an evil among all <hi type="italic">things</hi> that are done under the sun, that <hi type="italic">there is</hi> one event unto all: yea, also the heart of the sons of men is full of evil, and madness <hi type="italic">is</hi> in their heart while they live, and after that <hi type="italic">they go</hi> to the dead. <div eID="gen15060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15061" type="x-p"/> It has been observed concerning those who have pretended to search for the philosophers' stone that, though they could never find what they sought for, yet in the search they have hit upon many other useful discoveries and experiments. Thus Solomon, when, in the close of the foregoing chapter, he <hi type="italic">applied his heart to know the work of God,</hi> and took a great deal of pains to search into it, though he despaired of finding it out, yet he found out that which abundantly recompensed him for the search, and gave him some satisfaction, which he here gives us; <hi type="italic">for</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">he considered all this in his heart,</hi> and weighed it deliberately, that he might <hi type="italic">declare</hi> it for the good of others. Note, What we are <hi type="italic">to declare</hi> we should first <hi type="italic">consider;</hi> think twice before we speak once; and what we have <hi type="italic">considered</hi> we should then <hi type="italic">declare. I believed, therefore have I spoken.</hi> <div eID="gen15061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15062" type="x-p"/> The great difficulty which Solomon met with in studying the book of providence was the little difference that is made between good men and bad in the distribution of comforts and crosses, and the disposal of events. This has perplexed the minds of many wise and contemplative men. Solomon discourses of it in <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.1-Eccl.9.3">these verses</reference>, and, though he does not undertake to find out this <hi type="italic">work of God,</hi> yet he says that which may prevent its being a stumbling-block to us. <div eID="gen15062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15063" type="x-p"/> I. Before he describes the temptation in its strength he lays down a great and unquestionable truth, which he resolves to adhere to, and which, if firmly believed, will be sufficient to break the force of the temptation. This has been the way of God's people in grappling with this difficulty. Job, before he discourses of this matter, lays down the doctrine of God's omniscience (<reference osisRef="Job.24.1">Job xxiv. 1</reference>), Jeremiah the doctrine of his righteousness (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.1">Jer. xii. 1</reference>), another prophet that of his holiness (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.13">Hab. i. 13</reference>), the psalmist that of his goodness and peculiar favour to his own people (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.1">Ps. lxxiii. 1</reference>), and that is it which Solomon here fastens upon and resolves to abide by, that, though good and evil seem to be dispensed promiscuously, yet God has a particular care of and concern for his own people: <hi type="italic">The righteous and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God,</hi> under his special protection and guidance; all their affairs are managed by him for their good; all their wise and righteous actions <hi type="italic">are in his hand,</hi> to be recompensed in the other world, though not in this. They seem as if they were given up <hi type="italic">into the hand of their enemies,</hi> but it is not so. Men have <hi type="italic">no power against them but what is given them from above.</hi> The events that affect them do not come to pass by chance, but all according to the will and counsel of God, which will turn that to be for them which seemed to be most against them. Let this make us easy, whatever happens, that all God's saints are in his hand, <reference osisRef="Deut.33.3">Deut. xxxiii. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.10.29">John x. 29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.15">Ps. xxxi. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen15063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15064" type="x-p"/> II. He lays this down for a rule, that the love and hatred of God are not to be measured and judged of by men's outward condition. If prosperity were a certain sign of God's love, and affliction of his hatred, then it might justly be an offence to us to see the wicked and godly fare alike. But the matter is not so: <hi type="italic">No man knows either love or hatred by all that is before him</hi> in this world, by those things that are the objects of sense. These we may know by that which is within us; if we love God with all our heart, thereby we may know that he loves us, as we may know likewise that we are under his wrath if we be governed by that carnal mind which is enmity to him. These will be known by that which shall be hereafter, by men's everlasting state; it is certain that men are happy or miserable according as they are under the love or hatred of God, but not according as they are under the smiles or frowns of the world; and therefore if God loves a righteous man (as certainly he does) he is happy, though the world frown upon him; and if he hates a wicked man (as certainly he does) he is miserable, though the world smile upon him. Then the offence of this promiscuous distribution of events has ceased. <div eID="gen15064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15065" type="x-p"/> III. Having laid down these principles, he acknowledges that <hi type="italic">all things come alike to all;</hi> so it has been formerly, and therefore we are not to think it strange if it be so now, if it be so with us and our families. Some make this, and all that follows to <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.13">v. 13</reference>, to be the perverse reasoning of the atheists against the doctrine of God's providence; but I rather take it to be Solomon's concession, which he might the more freely make when he had fixed those truths which are sufficient to guard against any ill use that may be made of what he grants. Observe here (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.2">v. 2</reference>), <div eID="gen15065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15066" type="x-p"/> 1. The great difference that there is between the characters of the righteous and the wicked, which, in several instances, are set the one over-against the other, to show that, though <hi type="italic">all things come alike to all,</hi> yet that does not in the least confound the eternal distinction between moral good and evil, but that remains immutable. (1.) The righteous are <hi type="italic">clean,</hi> have <hi type="italic">clean hands and pure hearts;</hi> the wicked are <hi type="italic">unclean,</hi> under the dominion of unclean lusts, <hi type="italic">pure</hi> perhaps <hi type="italic">in their own eyes,</hi> but not <hi type="italic">cleansed from their filthiness,</hi> God will certainly put a difference <hi type="italic">between the clean and the unclean, the precious and the vile,</hi> in the other world, though he does not seem to do so in this. (2.) The righteous <hi type="italic">sacrifice,</hi> that is, they make conscience of worshipping God according to his will, both with inward and outward worship; the wicked <hi type="italic">sacrifice not,</hi> that is, they live in the neglect of God's worship and grudge to part with any thing for his honour. <hi type="italic">What is the Almighty, that they should serve him?</hi> (3.) The righteous are <hi type="italic">good,</hi> good in God's sight, they do good in the world; the wicked are <hi type="italic">sinners,</hi> violating the laws of God and man, and provoking to both. (4.) The wicked man <hi type="italic">swears,</hi> has no veneration for the name of God, but profanes it by swearing rashly and falsely; but the righteous man <hi type="italic">fears an oath,</hi> swears not, but is sworn, and then with great reverence; he fears to take an oath, because it is a solemn appeal to God as a witness and judge; he fears, when he has taken a oath, to break it, because God is righteous who takes vengeance. <div eID="gen15066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15067" type="x-p"/> 2. The little difference there is between the conditions of the righteous and the wicked in this world: <hi type="italic">There is one event to</hi> both. Is David rich? So is Nabal. Is Joseph favoured by his prince? So is Haman. Is Ahab killed in a battle? So is Josiah. Are the bad figs carried to Babylon? So are the good, <reference osisRef="Jer.24.1">Jer. xxiv. 1</reference>. There is a vast difference between the original, the design, and the nature, of the same event to the one and to the other; the effects and issues of it are likewise vastly different; the same providence to the one is <hi type="italic">a savour of life unto life,</hi> to the other <hi type="italic">of death unto death,</hi> though, to outward appearance, it is the same. <div eID="gen15067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15068" type="x-p"/> IV. He owns this to be a very great grievance to those that are wise and good: "<hi type="italic">This is an evil,</hi> the greatest perplexity, <hi type="italic">among all things that are done under the sun</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.3">v. 3</reference>); nothing has given me more disturbance than this, <hi type="italic">that there is one event unto all.</hi>" It hardens atheists, and strengthens the hands of evil-doers; for therefore it is that <hi type="italic">the hearts of the sons of men are full of evil</hi> and <hi type="italic">fully set in them to do evil,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.11">ch. viii. 11</reference>. When they see that <hi type="italic">there is one event to the righteous and the wicked</hi> they wickedly infer thence that it is all one to God whether they are righteous or wicked, and therefore they stick at nothing to gratify their lusts. <div eID="gen15068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15069" type="x-p"/> V. For the further clearing of this great difficulty, as he began this discourse with the doctrine of the happiness of the righteous (whatever they may suffer, they <hi type="italic">and their works are in the hands of God,</hi> and therefore in good hands, they could not be in better), so he concludes with the doctrine of the misery of the wicked; however they may prosper, <hi type="italic">madness is in their heart while they live, and after that they go to the dead.</hi> Envy not the prosperity of evil-doers, for, 1. They are now madmen, and all the delights they seem to be blessed with are but like the pleasant dreams and fancies of a distracted man. They are <hi type="italic">mad upon their idols</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.38">Jer. l. 38</reference>), are mad against God's people, <reference osisRef="Acts.26.11">Acts xxvi. 11</reference>. When the prodigal repented, it is said, <hi type="italic">He came to himself</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.17">Luke xv. 17</reference>), which intimates that he had been beside himself before. 2. They will shortly be dead men. They make a mighty noise and bustle <hi type="italic">while they live,</hi> but after awhile, <hi type="italic">they go to the dead,</hi> and there is an end of all their pomp and power; they will then be reckoned with for all their madness and outrage in sin. Though, on this side death, the righteous and the wicked seem alike, on the other side death there will be a vast difference between them.
entries.4dd39a4a08cc3f45496561e12219e93aa5c4edf2: <div eID="gen15069" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Consequences of Death; The Proper Enjoyment of Life.</title> <div sID="gen15070" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> For to him that is joined to all the living there is hope: for a living dog is better than a dead lion. <hi type="super">5</hi> For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten. <hi type="super">6</hi> Also their love, and their hatred, and their envy, is now perished; neither have they any more a portion for ever in any <hi type="italic">thing</hi> that is done under the sun. <hi type="super">7</hi> Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a merry heart; for God now accepteth thy works. <hi type="super">8</hi> Let thy garments be always white; and let thy head lack no ointment. <hi type="super">9</hi> Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest all the days of the life of thy vanity, which he hath given thee under the sun, all the days of thy vanity: for that <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy portion in <hi type="italic">this</hi> life, and in thy labour which thou takest under the sun. <hi type="super">10</hi> Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do <hi type="italic">it</hi> with thy might; for <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest. <div eID="gen15070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15071" type="x-p"/> Solomon, in a fret, had <hi type="italic">praised the dead more than the living</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.4.2">ch. iv. 2</reference>); but here, considering the advantages of life to prepare for death and make sure the hope of a better life, he seems to be of another mind. <div eID="gen15071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15072" type="x-p"/> I. He shows the advantages which the living have above those that are dead, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.4-Eccl.9.6">v. 4-6</reference>. 1. While there is life <hi type="italic">there is hope. Dum spiro, spero—While I breathe, I hope.</hi> It is the privilege of the living that they are <hi type="italic">joined to the living,</hi> in relation, commerce, and conversation, and, while they are so, <hi type="italic">there is hope.</hi> If a man's condition be, upon any account, bad, <hi type="italic">there is hope</hi> it will be amended. If <hi type="italic">the heart be full of evil, and madness be in it,</hi> yet while there is life <hi type="italic">there is hope</hi> that by the grace of God there may be a blessed change wrought; but after men <hi type="italic">go to the dead</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.3">v. 3</reference>) it is too late then; he that is then filthy will be filthy still, for ever filthy. If men be thrown aside as useless, yet, while they are <hi type="italic">joined to the living, there is hope</hi> that they may yet again take root and bear fruit; he that is alive is, or may be, good for something, but he that is dead, as to this world, is not capable of being any further serviceable. Therefore a <hi type="italic">living dog is better than a dead lion;</hi> the meanest beggar alive has that comfort of this world and does that service to it which the greatest prince, when he is dead, is utterly incapable of. 2. While there is life there is an opportunity of preparing for death: <hi type="italic">The living know</hi> that which the dead have no knowledge of, particularly they <hi type="italic">know that they shall die,</hi> and are, or may be, thereby influenced to prepare for that great change which will come certainly, and may come suddenly. Note, <hi type="italic">The living</hi> cannot but <hi type="italic">know that they shall die,</hi> that they must needs die. They know they are under a sentence of death; they are already taken into custody by its messengers, and feel themselves declining. This is a needful useful knowledge; for what is our business, while we live, but to get ready to die: <hi type="italic">The living know they shall die;</hi> it is a thing yet to come, and therefore provision may be made for it. The dead know they are dead, and it is too late; they are on the other side the great gulf fixed. 3. When life is gone all this world is gone with it, as to us. (1.) There is an end of all our acquaintance with this world and the things of it: <hi type="italic">The dead know not any thing</hi> of that which, while they lived, they were intimately conversant with. It does not appear that they know any thing of what is done by those they leave behind. Abraham is ignorant of us; they are removed <hi type="italic">into darkness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.10.22">Job x. 22</reference>. (2.) There is an end of all our enjoyments in this world: <hi type="italic">They have no more a reward</hi> for their toils about the world, but all they got must be left to others; they have a reward for their holy actions, but not for their worldly ones. The meats and the belly will be destroyed together, <reference osisRef="John.6.27">John vi. 27</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.13">1 Cor. vi. 13</reference>. It is explained <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.6">v. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">Neither have they any more a portion for ever,</hi> none of that which they imagined would be <hi type="italic">a portion for ever,</hi> of that which <hi type="italic">is done</hi> and got <hi type="italic">under the sun.</hi> The things of this world will not be a portion for the soul because they will not be a portion for ever; those that choose them, and have them for <hi type="italic">their good things,</hi> have only a <hi type="italic">portion in this life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Ps. xvii. 14</reference>. The world can only be an annuity for life, not a <hi type="italic">portion for ever.</hi> (3.) There is an end of their name. There are but few whose names survive them long; the grave is a land of forgetfulness, <hi type="italic">for the memory of those</hi> that are laid there <hi type="italic">is</hi> soon <hi type="italic">forgotten;</hi> their <hi type="italic">place knows them no more,</hi> nor the lands they called by their own names. (4.) There is an end of their affections, their friendships and enmities: <hi type="italic">Their love, and their hatred, and their envy have now perished;</hi> the good things they loved, the evil things they hated, the prosperity of others, which they envied, are now all at an end with them. Death parts those that loved one another, and puts an end to their friendship, and those that hated one another too, and puts an end to their quarrels. <hi type="italic">Actio moritur cum person&#226;—The person and his actions die together.</hi> There we shall be never the better for our friends (their love can do us no kindness), nor ever the worse for our enemies—their hatred and envy can do us no damage. <hi type="italic">There the wicked cease from troubling.</hi> Those things which now so affect us and fill us, which we are so concerned about and so jealous of, will there be at an end. <div eID="gen15072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15073" type="x-p"/> II. Hence he infers that it is our wisdom to make the best use of life that we can while it does last, and manage wisely what remains of it. <div eID="gen15073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15074" type="x-p"/> 1. Let us relish the comforts of life while we live, and cheerfully take our share of the enjoyments of it. Solomon, having been himself ensnared by the abuse of sensitive delights, warns others of the danger, not by a total prohibition of them, but by directing to the sober and moderate use of them; we may use the world, but must not abuse it, take what is to be had out of it, and expect no more. Here we have, <div eID="gen15074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15075" type="x-p"/> (1.) The particular instances of this cheerfulness prescribed: "Thou art drooping and melancholy, <hi type="italic">go thy way,</hi> like a fool as thou art, and get into a better temper of mind." [1.] "Let thy spirit be easy and pleasant; then let there be <hi type="italic">joy</hi> and <hi type="italic">a merry heart</hi> within," <hi type="italic">a good heart</hi> (so the word is), which distinguishes this from carnal mirth and sensual pleasure, which are the evil of the heart, both a symptom and a cause of much evil there. We must enjoy ourselves, enjoy our friends, enjoy our God, and be careful to keep a good conscience, that nothing may disturb us in these enjoyments. We must serve God with gladness, in the use of what he gives us, and be liberal in communicating it to others, and not suffer ourselves to be oppressed with inordinate care and grief about the world. We must eat our bread as Israelites, <hi type="italic">not in our mourning</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.26.14">Deut. xxvi. 14</reference>), as Christians, <hi type="italic">with gladness and</hi> liberality <hi type="italic">of heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.2.46">Acts ii. 46</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Deut.28.47">Deut. xxviii. 47</reference>. [2.] "Make use of the comforts and enjoyments which God has given thee: <hi type="italic">Eat thy bread, drink thy wine,</hi> thine, not another's, not <hi type="italic">the bread of deceit,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">the wine of violence,</hi> but that which is honestly got, else thou canst not eat it with any comfort nor expect a blessing upon it—<hi type="italic">thy bread</hi> and <hi type="italic">thy wine,</hi> such as are agreeable to thy place and station, not extravagantly above it nor sordidly below it; lay out what God has given thee for the ends for which thou art entrusted with it, as being but a steward." [3.] "Evidence thy cheerfulness (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let thy garments be always white.</hi> Observe a proportion in thy expenses; reduce not thy food in order to gratify thy pride, nor thy clothing in order to gratify thy voluptuousness. Be neat, wear clean linen, and be not slovenly." Or, "<hi type="italic">Let thy garments be white</hi> in token of joy and cheerfulness," which were expressed by <hi type="italic">white raiment</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.4">Rev. iii. 4</reference>); "and as a further token of joy, <hi type="italic">let thy head lack no ointment</hi> that is fit for it." Our Saviour admitted this piece of pleasure at a feast (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.7">Matt. xxvi. 7</reference>), and David observes it among the gifts of God's bounty to him. <reference osisRef="Ps.23.5">Ps. xxiii. 5</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thou anointest my head with oil.</hi> Not that we must place our happiness in any of the delights of sense, or set our hearts upon them, but what God has given us we must make as comfortable a use of as we can afford, under the limitations of sobriety and wisdom, and not forgetting the poor. [4.] "Make thyself agreeable to thy relations: <hi type="italic">Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest.</hi> Do not engross thy delights, making much of thyself only, and not caring what becomes of those about thee, but let them share with thee and make them easy too. Have a wife; for even in paradise <hi type="italic">it was not good for man to be alone.</hi> Keep to thy wife, to one, and do not multiply wives" (Solomon had found the mischief of that); "keep to her only, and have nothing to do with any other." How can a man live joyfully with one with whom he does not live honestly? "Love thy wife; and <hi type="italic">the wife whom thou lovest</hi> thou wilt be likely to <hi type="italic">live joyfully with.</hi>" When we do the duty of relations we may expect the comfort of them. See <reference osisRef="Prov.5.19">Prov. v. 19</reference>. "Live with thy wife, and delight in her society. <hi type="italic">Live joyfully with her,</hi> and be most cheerful when thou art with her. Take pleasure in thy family, thy vine and thy olive plants." <div eID="gen15075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15076" type="x-p"/> (2.) The qualifications necessary to this cheerfulness: "Rejoice and have <hi type="italic">a merry heart,</hi> if <hi type="italic">God now accepts thy works.</hi> If thou art reconciled to God, and recommended to him, then thou has reason to be cheerful, otherwise not." <hi type="italic">Rejoice not, O Israel! for joy, as other people, for thou hast gone a whoring from thy God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.9.1">Hos. ix. 1</reference>. Our first care must be to make our peace with God, and obtain his favour, to do that which he will accept of, and then, <hi type="italic">Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy.</hi> Note, Those whose works God has accepted have reason to be cheerful and ought to be so. 'Now that thou eatest the bread of thy sacrifices <hi type="italic">with joy,</hi> and partakest of the wine of thy drink-offerings <hi type="italic">with a merry heart,</hi> now <hi type="italic">God accepts thy works.</hi> Thy religious services, when performed with holy joy, are pleasing to God; he loves to have his servants sing at their work, it proclaims him a good Master. <div eID="gen15076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15077" type="x-p"/> (3.) The reasons for it. "Live joyfully, for," [1.] "It is all little enough to make thy passage through this world easy and comfortable: <hi type="italic">The days of thy life</hi> are the days <hi type="italic">of thy vanity;</hi> there is nothing here but trouble, and disappointment. Thou wilt have time enough for sorrow and grief when thou canst not help it, and therefore <hi type="italic">live joyfully</hi> while thou canst, and perplex not thyself with thoughts and cares about to-morrow; <hi type="italic">sufficient to the day is the evil thereof.</hi> Let a gracious serenity of mind be a powerful antidote against the vanity of the world." [2.] "It is all thou canst get from this world: <hi type="italic">That is thy portion in</hi> the things of <hi type="italic">this life.</hi> In God, and another life, thou shalt have a better portion, and a better recompence for thy labours in religion; but for thy pains <hi type="italic">which thou takest</hi> about the things <hi type="italic">under the sun</hi> this is all thou canst expect, and therefore do not deny this to thyself." <div eID="gen15077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15078" type="x-p"/> 2. Let us apply ourselves to the business of life while life lasts, and so use the enjoyments of it as by them to be fitted for the employments: "Therefore <hi type="italic">eat with joy</hi> and <hi type="italic">a merry heart,</hi> not that thy soul may take its ease (as <reference osisRef="Luke.12.19">Luke xii. 19</reference>), but that thy soul may take the more pains and the joy of the Lord may be its strength and oil to its wheels," <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.10">v. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">Whatsoever thy hand finds to do do it with thy might.</hi> Observe here, (1.) There is not only something to be had, but something to be done, in this life, and the chief good we are to enquire after is <hi type="italic">the good we should do,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.3">Eccl. ii. 3</reference>. This is the world of service; that to come is the world of recompence. This is the world of probation and preparation for eternity; we are here upon business, and upon our good behaviour. (2.) Opportunity is to direct and quicken duty. That is to be done which <hi type="italic">our hand finds to do,</hi> which occasion calls for; and an active hand will always find something to do that will turn to a good account. What must be done, of necessity, our hand will here find a price in it for the doing of, <reference osisRef="Prov.17.16">Prov. xvii. 16</reference>. (3.) What good we have an opportunity of doing we must do while we have the opportunity, and <hi type="italic">do it with our might,</hi> with care, vigour, and resolution, whatever difficulties and discouragements we may meet with in it. Harvest-days are busy days; and we must make hay while the sun shines. Serving God and working out our salvation must be done with <hi type="italic">all that is within us,</hi> and all little enough. (4.) There is good reason why we should <hi type="italic">work the works of him that sent us while it is day, because the night comes, wherein no man can work,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.9.4">John ix. 4</reference>. We must up and be doing now with all possible diligence, because our doing-time will be done shortly and we know not how soon. But this we know that, if the work of life be not done when our time is done, we are undone for ever: "<hi type="italic">There is no work</hi> to be done, <hi type="italic">nor device</hi> to do it, <hi type="italic">no knowledge</hi> for speculation, <hi type="italic">nor wisdom</hi> for practice, <hi type="italic">in the grave whither thou goest.</hi>" We are all going towards the grave; every day brings us a step nearer to it; when we are <hi type="italic">in the grave</hi> it will be too late to mend the errors of life, too late to repent and make our peace with God, too late to lay up any thing in store for eternal life; it must be done now or never. The grave is a land of darkness and silence, and therefore there is no doing any thing for our souls there; it must be done now or never, <reference osisRef="John.12.35">John xii. 35</reference>.
entries.d47c618b8e20b7754607dd5e3114f871c4309811: <div eID="gen15078" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Disappointment of Hopes.</title> <div sID="gen15079" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> I returned, and saw under the sun, that the race <hi type="italic">is</hi> not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all. <hi type="super">12</hi> For man also knoweth not his time: as the fishes that are taken in an evil net, and as the birds that are caught in the snare; so <hi type="italic">are</hi> the sons of men snared in an evil time, when it falleth suddenly upon them. <div eID="gen15079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15080" type="x-p"/> The preacher here, for a further proof of the vanity of the world, and to convince us that <hi type="italic">all our works are in the hand of God,</hi> and not in our own hand, shows the uncertainty and contingency of future events, and how often they contradict the prospects we have of them. He had exhorted us (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.10">v. 10</reference>) to do what we have to do <hi type="italic">with all our might;</hi> but here he reminds us that, when we have done all, we must leave the issue with God, and not be confident of the success. <div eID="gen15080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15081" type="x-p"/> I. We are often disappointed of the good we had great hopes of, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.11">v. 11</reference>. Solomon had himself made the observation, and so has many a one since, that events, both in public and private affairs, do not always agree even with the most rational prospects and probabilities. <hi type="italic">Nulli fortuna tam dedita est ut multa tentanti ubique respondeat</hi>—<hi type="italic">Fortune surrenders herself to no one so as to ensure him success, however numerous his undertakings.</hi> Seneca. The issue of affairs is often unaccountably cross to every one's expectation, that the highest may not presume, nor the lowest despair, but all may live in a humble dependence upon God, from whom every man's judgment proceeds. <div eID="gen15081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15082" type="x-p"/> 1. He gives instances of disappointment, even where means and instruments were most encouraging and promised fair. (1.) One would think that the lightest of foot should, in running, win the prize; and yet <hi type="italic">the race is not</hi> always <hi type="italic">to the swift;</hi> some accident happens to retard them, or they are too secure, and therefore remiss, and let those that are slower get the start of them. (2.) One would think that, in fighting, the most numerous and powerful army should be always victorious, and, in single combat, that the bold and mighty champion should win the laurel; but <hi type="italic">the battle is not</hi> always <hi type="italic">to the strong;</hi> a host of Philistines was once put to flight by Jonathan and his man; <hi type="italic">one of you shall chase a thousand;</hi> the goodness of the cause has often carried the day against the most formidable power. (3.) One would think that men of sense should always be men of substance, and that those who know how to live in the world should not only have a plentiful maintenance, but get great estates; and yet it does not always prove so; even <hi type="italic">bread is not</hi> always <hi type="italic">to the wise,</hi> much less <hi type="italic">riches</hi> always <hi type="italic">to men of understanding.</hi> Many ingenious men, and men of business, who were likely to thrive in the world, have strangely gone backward and come to nothing. (4.) One would think that those who understand men, and have the art of management, should always get preferment and obtain the smiles of great men; but many ingenious men have been disappointed, and have spent their days in obscurity, nay, have fallen into disgrace, and perhaps have ruined themselves by those very methods by which they hoped to raise themselves, for <hi type="italic">favour is not</hi> always <hi type="italic">to men of skill,</hi> but fools are favoured and wise men frowned upon. <div eID="gen15082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15083" type="x-p"/> 2. He resolves all these disappointments into an over-ruling power and providence, the disposals of which to us seem casual, and we call them <hi type="italic">chance,</hi> but really they are according to the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, here called <hi type="italic">time,</hi> in the language of this book, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.1">ch. iii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.15">Ps. xxxi. 15</reference>. <hi type="italic">Time and chance happen to them all.</hi> A sovereign Providence breaks men's measures, and blasts their hopes, and teaches them that the way of man is not in himself, but subject to the divine will. We must use means, but not trust to them; if we succeed, we must give God the praise (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.3">Ps. xliv. 3</reference>); if we be crossed, we must acquiesce in his will and take our lot. <div eID="gen15083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15084" type="x-p"/> II. We are often surprised with the evils we were in little fear of (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Man knows not his time,</hi> the time of his calamity, his fall, his death, which, in scripture, is called <hi type="italic">our day</hi> and <hi type="italic">our hour.</hi> 1. We know not what troubles are before us, which will take us off our business, and take us out of the world, what <hi type="italic">time and chance will happen to us,</hi> nor what <hi type="italic">one day,</hi> or a night, <hi type="italic">may bring forth.</hi> It is <hi type="italic">not for us to know the times,</hi> no, not our own time, when or how we shall die. God has, in wisdom, kept us in the dark, that we may be always ready. 2. Perhaps we may meet with trouble in that very thing wherein we promise ourselves the greatest satisfaction and advantage; as the fishes and the birds are drawn into the snare and net by the bait laid to allure them, which they greedily catch at, so are the sons of men often <hi type="italic">snared in an evil time,</hi> when it falls suddenly upon them, before they are aware. And these things too <hi type="italic">come alike to all.</hi> Men often find their bane where they sought their bless, and catch their death where they thought to find a prize. Let us therefore never be secure, but always ready for changes, that, though they may be sudden, they may be no surprise or terror to us.
entries.af8dc225556be04c9b93f5d40a66e6037ced56d3: <div eID="gen15084" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Advantages of Wisdom.</title> <div sID="gen15085" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> This wisdom have I seen also under the sun, and it <hi type="italic">seemed</hi> great unto me: <hi type="super">14</hi> <hi type="italic">There was</hi> a little city, and few men within it; and there came a great king against it, and besieged it, and built great bulwarks against it: 15 Now there was found in it a poor wise man, and he by his wisdom delivered the city; yet no man remembered that same poor man. <hi type="super">16</hi> Then said I, Wisdom <hi type="italic">is</hi> better than strength: nevertheless the poor man's wisdom <hi type="italic">is</hi> despised, and his words are not heard. <hi type="super">17</hi> The words of wise <hi type="italic">men are</hi> heard in quiet more than the cry of him that ruleth among fools. 18 Wisdom <hi type="italic">is</hi> better than weapons of war: but one sinner destroyeth much good. <div eID="gen15085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15086" type="x-p"/> Solomon still recommends wisdom to us as necessary to the preserving of our peace and the perfecting of our business, notwithstanding the vanities and crosses which human affairs are subject to. He had said (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.11">v. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">Bread is not always to the wise;</hi> yet he would not therefore be thought either to disparage, or to discourage, wisdom, no, he still retains his principle, that <hi type="italic">wisdom excels folly as much as light excels darkness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.13">ch. ii. 13</reference>), and we ought to love and embrace it, and be governed by it, for the sake of its own intrinsic worth, and the capacity it gives us of being serviceable to others, though we ourselves should not get wealth and preferment by it. This wisdom, that is, this which he here describes, wisdom which enables a man to serve his country out of pure affection to its interests, when he himself gains no advantage by it, no, not so much as thanks for his pains, or the reputation of it, this is the wisdom which, Solomon says, <hi type="italic">seemed great unto him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.13">v. 13</reference>. A public spirit, in a private sphere, is wisdom which those who understand things that differ cannot but look upon as very magnificent. <div eID="gen15086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15087" type="x-p"/> I. Solomon here gives an instance, which probably was a case in fact, in some neighbouring country, of a <hi type="italic">poor man</hi> who with his wisdom did great service in a time of public distress and danger (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">There was a little city</hi> (no great prize, whoever was master of it); there were but <hi type="italic">few men within it,</hi> to defend it, and men, if men of fortitude, are the best fortifications of a city; here were <hi type="italic">few men,</hi> and, because few, feeble, fearful, and ready to give up their city as not tenable. Against this little city a <hi type="italic">great king</hi> came with a numerous army, and besieged it, either in pride, or covetousness to possess it, or in revenge for some affront given him, to chastise and destroy it. Thinking it stronger than it was, he <hi type="italic">built great bulwarks against it,</hi> from which to batter it, and doubted not but in a little time to make himself master of it. What a great deal of unjust vexation do ambitious princes give to their harmless neighbours! This <hi type="italic">great king</hi> needed not fear this <hi type="italic">little city;</hi> why then should he frighten it? It would be little profit to him; why then should he put himself to such a great expense to gain it? But as unreasonable and insatiably greedy as little people sometimes are to <hi type="italic">lay house to house, and field to field,</hi> great kings often are to lay city to city, and province to province, <hi type="italic">that they may be placed alone in the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.5.8">Isa. v. 8</reference>. Did victory and success attend the <hi type="italic">strong?</hi> No; there was found in this little city, among the few men that were in it, <hi type="italic">one poor wise man</hi>—a wise man, and yet poor, and not preferred to any place of profit or power in the city; places of trust were not given to men according to their merit, and meetness for them, else such a wise man as this would not have been a poor man. Now, 1. Being wise, he served the city, though he was poor. In their distress they found him out (<reference osisRef="Judg.11.7">Judg. xi. 7</reference>) and begged his advice and assistance; and <hi type="italic">he by his wisdom delivered the city,</hi> either by prudent instructions given to the besieged, directing them to some unthought-of stratagem for their own security, or by a prudent treaty with the besiegers, as the woman at Abel, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.16">2 Sam. xx. 16</reference>. He did not upbraid them with the contempt they had put upon him, in leaving him out of their council, nor tell them he was poor and had nothing to lose, and therefore cared not what became of the city; but he did his best for it, and was blessed with success. Note, Private interests and personal resentments must always be sacrificed to public good and forgotten when the common welfare is concerned. 2. Being poor, he was slighted by the city, though he was wise and had been an instrument to save them all from ruin: <hi type="italic">No man remembered that same poor man;</hi> his good services were not taken notice of, no recompence was made him, no marks of honour were put upon him, but he lived in as much poverty and obscurity as he had done before. <hi type="italic">Riches were not</hi> to this <hi type="italic">man of understanding,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">favour to</hi> this <hi type="italic">man of skill.</hi> Many who have well-merited of their prince and country have been ill-paid; such an ungrateful world do we live in. It is well that useful men have a God to trust to, who will be their bountiful rewarder; for, among men, great services are often envied and rewarded with evil for good. <div eID="gen15087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15088" type="x-p"/> II. From this instance he draws some useful inferences, looks upon it and receives instruction. 1. Hence he observes the great usefulness and excellency of wisdom, and what a blessing it makes men to their country: <hi type="italic">Wisdom is better than strength,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.16">v. 16</reference>. A prudent mind, which is the honour of a man, is to be preferred before a robust body, in which many of the brute creatures excel man. A man may by his wisdom effect that which he could never compass by his strength, and may overcome those by out-witting them who are able to overpower him. Nay, <hi type="italic">wisdom is better than weapons of war,</hi> offensive or defensive, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.18">v. 18</reference>. <hi type="italic">Wisdom,</hi> that is, religion and piety (for the wise man is here opposed to a sinner), is better than all military endowments or accoutrements, for it will engage God for us, and then we are safe in the greatest perils and successful in the greatest enterprises. <hi type="italic">If God be for us, who can be against us</hi> or stand before us? 2. Hence he observes the commanding force and power of wisdom, though it labour under external disadvantages (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">The words of wise men are heard in quiet;</hi> what they speak, being spoken calmly and with deliberation (though, not being rich and in authority, they dare not speak aloud nor with any great assurance), will be hearkened to and regarded, will gain respect, nay, will gain the point, and sway with men more than the imperious clamour of him that <hi type="italic">rules among fools,</hi> who, like fools, chose him to be their ruler, for his noise and blustering, and, like fools, think he must by those methods carry the day with every body else. A few close arguments are worth a great many big words; and those will strike sail to fair reasoning who will answer those that hector and insult <hi type="italic">according to their folly. How forcible are right words!</hi> What is spoken wisely should be spoken calmly, and then it will be heard in quiet and calmly considered. But passion will lessen the force even of reason, instead of adding any force to it. 3. Hence he observes that wise and good men, notwithstanding this, must often content themselves with the satisfaction of having done good, or at least attempted it, and offered at it, when they cannot do the good they would do nor have the praise they should have. Wisdom capacitates a man to serve his neighbours, and he offers his service; but, alas! if he be poor his wisdom is despised and <hi type="italic">his words are not heard,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.16">v. 16</reference>. Many a man is buried alive in poverty and obscurity who, if he had but fit encouragement given him, might be a great blessing to the world; many a pearl is lost in its shell. But there is a day coming when wisdom and goodness shall be in honour, and the <hi type="italic">righteous shall shine forth.</hi> <div eID="gen15088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15089" type="x-p"/> 4. From what he had observed of the great good which one wise and virtuous man may do he infers what a great deal of mischief one wicked man may do, and what a great deal of good he may be the hindrance of: <hi type="italic">One sinner destroyeth much good.</hi> (1.) As to himself, a sinful condition is a wasteful condition. How many of the good gifts both of nature and Providence does one sinner destroy and make waste of—good sense, good parts, good learning, a good disposition, a good estate, good meat, good drink, and abundance of God's good creatures, all made use of in the service of sin, and so destroyed and lost, and the end of giving them frustrated and perverted! He who destroys his own soul destroys much good. (2.) As to others, what a great deal of mischief may one wicked man do in a town or country! One sinner, who makes it his business to debauch others, may defeat and frustrate the intentions of a great many good laws and a great deal of good preaching, and draw many into his pernicious ways; one sinner may be the ruin of a town, as one Achan troubled the whole camp of Israel. The wise man who delivered the city would have had his due respect and recompence for it but that some one sinner hindered it, and invidiously diminished the service. And many a good project, well laid for the public welfare, had been destroyed by some one subtle adversary to it. The wisdom of some would have healed the nation, but, through the wickedness of a few, it would not be healed. See who are a kingdom's friends and enemies, if one saint does much good, and one sinner destroys much good.  <chapter eID="Eccl.9"/> <div eID="gen15089" type="x-p"/>

No man knoweth either the love or hatred (of God to them) by all that is before them," that is, by what is outwardly seen in His present dealings (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.14">Ec 8:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.17">17</reference>). However, from the sense of the same words, in <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.6">Ec 9:6</reference>, "love and hatred" seem to be the feelings of the wicked towards the righteous, whereby they caused to the latter comfort or sorrow. Translate: "Even the love and hatred" (exhibited towards the righteous, are in God's hand) (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.10">Psa 76:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.16.7">Pr 16:7</reference>). "No man knoweth all that is before them." <div eID="gen12669" type="x-p"/>

All things ... alike--</hi>not universally; but as to death. <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.2-Eccl.9.10">Ec 9:2-10</reference> are made by Holden the objection of a skeptical sensualist. Translate, "There is an evil above all (evils) that are done," &c., namely, that not only "there is one event to all," but "also the heart of the sons of men" makes this fact a reason for "madly" persisting in "evil while they live, and after that," &c., sin is "madness."<div eID="gen12676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12677" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the dead--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.2.18">Pr 2:18</reference>; 9:18). <div eID="gen12677" type="x-p"/>

For--</hi>rather, "Nevertheless." English Version rightly reads as the Margin, Hebrew, "that is joined," instead of the text, "who is to be chosen?"<div eID="gen12678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12679" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hope--</hi>not of mere temporal good (<reference osisRef="Job.14.7">Job 14:7</reference>); but of yet repenting and being saved.<div eID="gen12679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12680" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dog--</hi>metaphor for the vilest persons (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.14">1Sa 24:14</reference>).<div eID="gen12680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12681" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lion--</hi>the noblest of animals (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.30">Pr 30:30</reference>).<div eID="gen12681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12682" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">better--</hi>as to hope of salvation; the noblest who die unconverted have no hope; the vilest, so long as they have life, have hope. <div eID="gen12682" type="x-p"/>
entries.f6e17e7c60ea8cc5e58234bad073f75b99c04b28: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8135"/><div sID="gen12683" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8135"/><hi type="bold">5. know that they shall die--</hi>and may thereby be led "so to number their days, that they may apply their hearts to wisdom" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.1-Eccl.7.4">Ec 7:1-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.90.12">Psa 90:12</reference>).<div eID="gen12683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12684" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dead know not anything--</hi>that is, so far as their bodily senses and worldly affairs are concerned (<reference osisRef="Job.14.21">Job 14:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.16">Is 63:16</reference>); also, they know no door of repentance open to them, such as is to all on earth.<div eID="gen12684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12685" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither ... reward--</hi>no advantage from their worldly labors (Ec 2:18-22; 4:9).<div eID="gen12685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12686" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">memory--</hi>not of the righteous (<reference osisRef="Ps.112.6">Psa 112:6</reference>; Mal 3:16), but the wicked, who with all the pains to perpetuate their names (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.11">Psa 49:11</reference>) are soon "forgotten" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.10">Ec 8:10</reference>). <div eID="gen12686" type="x-p"/>
entries.a12092983d8437ee98e0f399247a09d905d4bd7a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8136"/><div sID="gen12687" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8136"/><hi type="bold">6. love, and ... hatred, &c.--</hi>(referring to <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.1">Ec 9:1</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.1">Ec 9:1</reference>). Not that these cease in a future world absolutely (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.27">Eze 32:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.11">Re 22:11</reference>); but as the end of this verse shows, relatively to persons and things in this world. Man's love and hatred can no longer be exercised for good or evil in the same way as here; but the fruits of them remain. What he is at death he remains for ever. "Envy," too, marks the wicked as referred to, since it was therewith that they assailed the righteous (see on <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.1">Ec 9:1</reference>).<div eID="gen12687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12688" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">portion--</hi>Their "portion" was "in this life" (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Psa 17:14</reference>), that they now "cannot have any more." <div eID="gen12688" type="x-p"/>
entries.1d6e9970e29f0c8d19455a5bd2aa5620eb8db8a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8137"/><div sID="gen12689" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8137"/>7. Addressed to the "righteous wise," spoken of in <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.1">Ec 9:1</reference>. Being "in the hand of God," who now accepteth "thy works" in His service, as He has previously accepted thy person (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.4">Ge 4:4</reference>), thou mayest "eat ... with a cheerful (not sensually 'merry') heart" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.13">Ec 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.18">5:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.46">Ac 2:46</reference>). <div eID="gen12689" type="x-p"/>
entries.550d2e41051cffc7177e31ef0826ec66a1366dea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8138"/><div sID="gen12690" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8138"/><hi type="bold">8. white--</hi>in token of joy (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">Is 61:3</reference>). Solomon was clad in white (Josephus, Antiquities, 8:7,3); hence his attire is compared to the "lilies" (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.29">Mt 6:29</reference>), typical of the spotless righteousness of Jesus Christ, which the redeemed shall wear (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.18">Re 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.7.14">7:14</reference>).<div eID="gen12690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12691" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ointment--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.23.5">Psa 23:5</reference>), opposed to a gloomy exterior (<reference osisRef="2Sam.14.2">2Sa 14:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.45.7">Psa 45:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.6.17">Mt 6:17</reference>); typical, also (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.1">Ec 7:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.1.3">So 1:3</reference>). <div eID="gen12691" type="x-p"/>
entries.95de5e99e6032fefcdd4382cb3c3d97c3fea4af2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8139"/><div sID="gen12692" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8139"/><hi type="bold">9. wife ... lovest--</hi>godly and true love, opposed to the "snares" of the "thousand" concubines (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.26">Ec 7:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.28">28</reference>), "among" whom Solomon could not find the true love which joins one man to one woman (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.15">Pr 5:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.18.19">18, 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.18.22">18:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.19.14">19:14</reference>). <div eID="gen12692" type="x-p"/>
entries.1c090bb6e9164e6cda6174342abc4755bcfeb0e3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8140"/><div sID="gen12693" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8140"/><hi type="bold">10. Whatsoever--</hi>namely, in the service of God. This and last verse plainly are the language of Solomon, not of a skeptic, as Holden would explain it.<div eID="gen12693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12694" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hand, &c.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Lev.12.8">Le 12:8</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.7">1Sa 10:7</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen12694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12695" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy might--</hi>diligence (<reference osisRef="Deut.6.5">De 6:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.10">Jr 48:10</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen12695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12696" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no work ... in the grave--</hi>(<reference osisRef="John.9.4">Joh 9:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.14.13">Re 14:13</reference>). "The soul's play-day is Satan's work-day; the idler the man the busier the tempter" [South]. <div eID="gen12696" type="x-p"/>
entries.11081c2241ced5c05f0d695f84714af051661fc9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8141"/><div sID="gen12697" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8141"/>11. This verse qualifies the sentiment, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.7-Eccl.9.9">Ec 9:7-9</reference>. Earthly "enjoyments," however lawful in their place (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.1">Ec 3:1</reference>), are to give way when any work to be done for God requires it. Reverting to the sentiment (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.17">Ec 8:17</reference>), we ought, therefore, not only to work God's work "with might" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.10">Ec 9:10</reference>), but also with the feeling that the event is wholly "in God's hand" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.1">Ec 9:1</reference>).<div eID="gen12697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12698" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">race ... not to the swift--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Sam.18.23">2Sa 18:23</reference>); spiritually (<reference osisRef="Zeph.3.19">Zep 3:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.16">Ro 9:16</reference>).<div eID="gen12698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12699" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nor ... battle to ... strong--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.47">1Sa 17:47</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.9">2Ch 14:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.15">11, 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.33.16">Psa 33:16</reference>).<div eID="gen12699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12700" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bread--</hi>livelihood.<div eID="gen12700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12701" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">favour--</hi>of the great.<div eID="gen12701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12702" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chance--</hi>seemingly, really Providence. But as man cannot "find it out" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.11">Ec 3:11</reference>), he needs "with all might" to use opportunities. Duties are ours; events, God's. <div eID="gen12702" type="x-p"/>
entries.bf3356d44873e4ab6f714a2f867ce7b54772633e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8142"/><div sID="gen12703" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8142"/><hi type="bold">12. his time--</hi>namely, of death (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15">Ec 7:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.13.22">Is 13:22</reference>). Hence the danger of delay in doing the work of God, as one knows not when his opportunity will end (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.10">Ec 9:10</reference>).<div eID="gen12703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12704" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">evil net--</hi>fatal to them. The unexpected suddenness of the capture is the point of comparison. So the second coming of Jesus Christ, "as a snare" (<reference osisRef="Luke.21.35">Lu 21:35</reference>).<div eID="gen12704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12705" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">evil time--</hi>as an "evil net," fatal to them. <div eID="gen12705" type="x-p"/>
entries.48b33795ff2f59e34e40893796a6c78047fd57bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8143"/><div sID="gen12706" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8143"/>13. Rather, "I have seen wisdom of this kind also," that is, exhibited in the way which is described in what follows [Maurer]. <div eID="gen12706" type="x-p"/>
entries.9addfa44a4f040850c7e5e9b31f43ab81db67e81: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8144"/><div sID="gen12707" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8144"/>14-15. (<reference osisRef="2Sam.20.16-2Sam.20.22">2Sa 20:16-22</reference>).<div eID="gen12707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12708" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bulwarks--</hi>military works of besiegers. <div eID="gen12708" type="x-p"/>
entries.6d7ec41c76cbff1c60a176443aa969be552ee540: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8146"/><div sID="gen12711" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8146"/>16. Resuming the sentiment (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.19">Ec 7:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.21.22">Pr 21:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.5">24:5</reference>).<div eID="gen12711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12712" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">poor man's wisdom is despised--</hi>not the poor man mentioned in <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.15">Ec 9:15</reference>; for his wisdom could not have saved the city, had "his words not been heard"; but poor men in general. So Paul (<reference osisRef="Acts.27.11">Ac 27:11</reference>). <div eID="gen12712" type="x-p"/>
entries.58a1a6ecfa7d104794268305da28c2a7096f6dd8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8147"/><div sID="gen12713" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8147"/><hi type="bold">17. The words of wise, &c.--</hi>Though generally the poor wise man is not heard (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.16">Ec 9:16</reference>), yet "the words of wise men, when heard in quiet (when calmly given heed to, as in <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.15">Ec 9:15</reference>), are more serviceable than," &c.<div eID="gen12713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12714" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ruleth--</hi>as the "great king" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.14">Ec 9:14</reference>). Solomon reverts to "the rulers to their own hurt" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.9">Ec 8:9</reference>). <div eID="gen12714" type="x-p"/>
entries.36e6460c56a2fb050bd7cff631acbd8ad42afe9d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8148"/><div sID="gen12715" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8148"/><hi type="bold">18. one sinner, &c.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Josh.7.1">Jos 7:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.12">11, 12</reference>). Though wisdom excels folly (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.16">Ec 9:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.19">7:19</reference>), yet a "little folly (equivalent to sin) can destroy much good," both in himself (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.1">Ec 10:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.2.10">Jas 2:10</reference>) and in others. "Wisdom" must, from the antithesis to "sinner," mean religion. Thus typically, the "little city" may be applied to the Church (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.32">Lu 12:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.22">He 12:22</reference>); the great king to Satan (<reference osisRef="John.12.31">Joh 12:31</reference>); the despised poor wise man, Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.2">Is 53:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.6.3">Mr 6:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.9">2Co 8:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.7">Ep 1:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.3">Col 2:3</reference>). <chapter eID="Eccl.9"/>

entries.96edf9fa0836ff6a46ff6f65b0674faa6b6f4324: <div eID="gen25608" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen25609" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25610" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25610" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25609" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25611" type="x-p"/> No men knows, by any present sign, what is before him, <reference osisRef="Ecc.9.1">Ecc 9:1</reference>. All things happen alike to all, <reference osisRef="Ecc.9.2">Ecc 9:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ecc.9.3">Ecc 9:3</reference>. Comparison of the state of the dead and the living, <reference osisRef="Ecc.9.4-Ecc.9.6">Ecc 9:4-6</reference>. Enjoy God's mercies, and live to his glory, <reference osisRef="Ecc.9.7-Ecc.9.10">Ecc 9:7-10</reference>. The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, <reference osisRef="Ecc.9.11">Ecc 9:11</reference>. Man is ignorant of futurity, <reference osisRef="Ecc.9.12">Ecc 9:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ecc.9.13">Ecc 9:13</reference>. The account of the little city, and the poor wise man, <reference osisRef="Ecc.9.14-Ecc.9.18">Ecc 9:14-18</reference>. <div eID="gen25611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25612" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen25612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25613" type="x-p"/> The righteous, and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God - This is a continuation of the preceding subject; and here the wise man draws a conclusion from what he had seen, and from the well-known character of God, that the righteous, the wise, and their conduct, were all in the hand of God, protected by his power, and safe in his approbation: but we cannot judge from the occurrences which take place in life who are the objects of God's love or displeasure.
entries.3142273fbe3af662b766257e6b7195620f89b7fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen25613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25614" type="x-p"/> All things come alike to all - This is very generally true; but God often makes a difference and his faithful followers witness many interventions of Divine Providence in their behalf. But there are general blessings, and general natural evils, that equally affect the just and the unjust. But in this all is right; the evils that are in nature are the effects of the Fall of man; and God will not suspend general laws, or alter them, to favor individual cases. Nor does he design that his approbation or disapprobation shall be shown by any of these occurrences. Every holy man has a testimony of God's approbation in his own heart; and this makes him truly happy, let outward things be as they may. And, in general, what the wicked suffer is the fruit of their own doings. But the general state of nature as to what are called natural evils, is just as it ought to be. There is evil enough to show that man has fallen from God, and good enough to show that God deals with him in mercy. I cannot see that there is any rational cause for me to stumble at the dispensations of Divine Providence on these accounts.
entries.c76294479e97965116d2c788b9419c7934d632b0: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen25614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25615" type="x-p"/> The heart of the sons of men is full of evil - No wonder then that the curse of God should be frequent in the earth.
entries.6958db7c244680d45641aaf37e457dbba83d5d76: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen25615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25616" type="x-p"/> For to him that is joined to all the living there is hope - While a man lives he hopes to amend, and he hopes to have a better lot; and thus life is spent, hoping to grow better, and hoping to get more. The Vulgate has, "There is none that shall live always, nor has any hope of such a thing." Perhaps the best translation is the following: "What, therefore, is to be chosen? In him that is living there is hope." Then choose that eternal life which thou hopest to possess. <div eID="gen25616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25617" type="x-p"/> A living dog is better than a dead lion - I suppose this was a proverb. The smallest measure of animal existence is better than the largest of dead matter. The poorest living peasant is infinitely above Alexander the Great.
entries.57012e798bb363dc51b051c69c4da3bdff423207: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen25617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25618" type="x-p"/> The living know that they shall die - This is so self-evident that none can doubt it; and therefore all that have this conviction should prepare for death and eternal blessedness. <div eID="gen25618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25619" type="x-p"/> But the dead know not any thing - Cut off from life, they know nothing of what passes under the sun. Their day of probation is ended, and therefore they can have no farther reward in living a holy life; nor can they be liable to any farther punishment for crimes in a state of probation, that being ended.
entries.4a57852b42086206d9e2382f4d859a1e1088c5c0: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen25619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25620" type="x-p"/> Also their love, and their hatred - It is evident that he speaks here of the ignorance, want of power, etc., of the dead, in reference only to this life. And though they have no more a portion under the sun, yet he does not intimate that they have none anywhere else. A man threatens to conquer kingdoms, etc. He dies; what are his threats?
entries.d33a79dcdf7cb6c3e3bd9cdb464dfb8026cbb13f: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen25620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25621" type="x-p"/> Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy - Do not vex and perplex yourselves with the dispensations and mysteries of Providence; enjoy the blessings which God has given you, and live to his glory; and then God will accept your works.
entries.441cc320f8bc3cf3da4adacdb74c842c484d1bc8: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen25621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25622" type="x-p"/> Let thy garments be always white - The Jews wore white garments on festal occasions, as emblems of joy and innocence. Be always pure, and always happy. The inhabitants of India are all dressed in clean white cotton, and to this is the allusion in the text. <div eID="gen25622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25623" type="x-p"/> The Targum says: "At all times let thy garments be washed and pure from the stain of sin. Acquire a good name, which is likened to the oil of anointing, that blessings may be called down up thy head, and goodness not forsake thee."
entries.8c1c9bbe9127128bb8536e38df406bff09ed424d: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen25623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25624" type="x-p"/> Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest - Marry prudently, keep faithfully attached to the wife thou hast chosen, and rejoice in the labor of thy hands. <div eID="gen25624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25625" type="x-p"/> Some understand this as the words of the libertine objector: "Live joyfully with the woman whom thou lovest best." But this does not comport so well with the scope of the place.
entries.6ab864e43376cda8043fbf0c1d95f288fbb1c485: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen25625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25626" type="x-p"/> Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do - Examine here the What the How, and the Why. <div eID="gen25626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25627" type="x-p"/> I. What is necessary to be done in this life, in reference to another? <div eID="gen25627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25628" type="x-p"/> 1. Turn from sin. <div eID="gen25628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25629" type="x-p"/> 2. Repent. <div eID="gen25629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25630" type="x-p"/> 3. Frequent the ordinances of God, and associate with the upright. <div eID="gen25630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25631" type="x-p"/> 4. Read the Scriptures. <div eID="gen25631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25632" type="x-p"/> 5. Pray for pardon. <div eID="gen25632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25633" type="x-p"/> 6. Believe on the Lord Jesus, that thou mayest obtain it. <div eID="gen25633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25634" type="x-p"/> 7. Look for the gift of the Holy Spirit. <div eID="gen25634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25635" type="x-p"/> 8. Bring forth in their seasons the fruits of it - (1) Repentance, (2) Faith; and (3) The Holy Spirit. <div eID="gen25635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25636" type="x-p"/> 9. Live to get good. <div eID="gen25636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25637" type="x-p"/> 10. And to do good. <div eID="gen25637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25638" type="x-p"/> 11. And refer every purpose and act to the eternal world. <div eID="gen25638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25639" type="x-p"/> II. How should these be done? With thy might. <div eID="gen25639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25640" type="x-p"/> 1. Be fully convinced of the necessity of these things. <div eID="gen25640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25641" type="x-p"/> 2. Be determined to act according to this conviction. <div eID="gen25641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25642" type="x-p"/> 3. Then act with all thy strength; put forth all thy power in avoiding evil, repenting of sin, etc., etc. <div eID="gen25642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25643" type="x-p"/> III. Why should this be done? <div eID="gen25643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25644" type="x-p"/> 1. Because thou art a dying man. <div eID="gen25644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25645" type="x-p"/> 2. Thou art going into the grave. <div eID="gen25645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25646" type="x-p"/> 3. When thou leavest this life, thy state of probation, with all its advantages, is eternally ended. <div eID="gen25646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25647" type="x-p"/> 4. If thou die in sin, where God is thou shalt never come. For, <div eID="gen25647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25648" type="x-p"/> 1. There is no work by which thou mayest profit; <div eID="gen25648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25649" type="x-p"/> 2. No device by which thou mayest escape punishment; <div eID="gen25649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25650" type="x-p"/> 3. No knowledge of any means of help; and, <div eID="gen25650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25651" type="x-p"/> 4. No wisdom - restoration of the soul to the favor and image of God, in that grave whither thou goest. Therefore, work while it is called to-day. <div eID="gen25651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25652" type="x-p"/> My old MS. Bible translates this nervously: Whatever thinge may thin hond don, besily wirch: for nouther were, ne resoun, ne wisdom, ne keennyng schuln be a nentis hell, whither thou gost. Properly speaking, every sinner is going to hell, and the wisdom of God calls upon him to turn and live.
entries.296c3f9f527adc7d7dc036830a5223b02e1fa51b: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen25652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25653" type="x-p"/> The race is not to the swift - It is not by swiftness, nor by strength and valor, that races are gained and battles won. God causes the lame often to take the prey, the prize; and so works that the weak overthrow the strong; therefore, no man should confide in himself. All things are under the government, and at the disposal of God. <div eID="gen25653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25654" type="x-p"/> But time and chance - עת eth, time or opportunity, and פגע pega, incident or occurrence: - <div eID="gen25654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25655" type="x-p"/> Happeneth to them all - Every man has what may be called time and space to act in, and opportunity to do a particular work. But in this Time and Opportunity there is Incident, what may fall in; and Occurrence, what may meet and frustrate an attempt. These things should be wisely weighed, and seriously balanced; for those four things belong to every human action. While you have Time, seek an Opportunity to do what is right; but calculate on hinderances and oppositions, because time and opportunity have their Incident and Occurrence. Coverdale translates this verse well: "I sawe that in runnynge, it helpeth not to be swift; in batayll, it helpeth not to be stronge; to fedynge, it helpeth not to be wyse; to riches, it helpeth not to be sutyll; to be had in favoure, it helpeth not to be connynge; but that all lyeth in time and fortune."
entries.bd79332e9d7e4ad0943098771455de5fbc69c8b7: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen25655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25656" type="x-p"/> As the birds that are caught - Man acts so heedlessly, notwithstanding all his wisdom, and all his warnings, that he is often taken, as a fish is, by the baited hook; and the bird by the baited snare. And thus, an evil time, like the snare, gin, trap, hook, falleth suddenly upon them; and they are taken in a moment, and have no means of escaping. How frequently do we see these comparisons illustrated!
entries.61c51827cc4215b321b783e138290fa8e2fc37eb: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen25656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25657" type="x-p"/> There was a little city, and few men within it - Here is another proof of the vanity of sublunary things; the ingratitude of men, and the little compensation that genuine merit receives. The little history mentioned here may have either been a fact, or intended as an instructive fable. A little city, with few to defend it, being besieged by a great king and a powerful army, was delivered by the cunning and address on a poor wise man; and afterwards his townsmen forgot their obligation to him. <div eID="gen25657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25658" type="x-p"/> Those who spiritualize this passage, making the little city the Church, the few men the Apostles, the great king the Devil, and the poor wise man Jesus Christ, abuse the text. <div eID="gen25658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25659" type="x-p"/> But the Targum is not less whimsical: "The little city is the human body; few men in it, few good affections to work righteousness; the great king, evil concupiscence, which, like a strong and powerful king, enters into the body to oppress it, and besieges the heart so as to cause it to err; built great bulwarks against it - evil concupiscence builds his throne in it wheresoever he wills, and causes it to decline from the ways that are right before God; that it may be taken in the greatest nets of hell, that he may burn it seven times, because of its sins. But there is found in it a poor wise man - a good, wise, and holy affection, which prevails over the evil principle, and snatches the body from the judgment of hell, by the strength of its wisdom. Yet, after this deliverance, the man did not remember what the good principle had done for him; but said in his heart, I am innocent," etc. <div eID="gen25659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25660" type="x-p"/> What a wonderful text has this been in the hands of many a modern Targumist; and with what force have the Keachonians preached Christ crucified from it! <div eID="gen25660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25661" type="x-p"/> Such a passage as this receives a fine illustration from the case of Archimedes saving the city of Syracuse from all the Roman forces besieging it by sea ana land. He destroyed their ships by his burning-glasses, lifted up their galleys out of the water by his machines, dashing some to pieces, and sinking others. One man's wisdom here prevailed for a long time against the most powerful exertions of a mighty nation. In this case, wisdom far exceeded strength. But was not Syracuse taken, notwithstanding the exertions of this poor wise man? No. But it was betrayed by the baseness of Mericus, a Spaniard, one of the Syracusan generals.
